scores.evidence: GitHub expects webhook replies within about 10 s... changing them forces every installation to re-approve
scores.rationale: GitHub App mechanics (permission re-approval, HMAC verification, installation token lifetimes, webhook timing, branch protection enforced server-side), gVisor, SKIP LOCKED queues and injection realities are all stated accurately, including the subtle parts the design depends on.

scores.evidence: triages them (labels, priority, duplicates, requests for info...) and for issues a maintainer approves, writes a fix in a sandbox and opens a draft PR
scores.rationale: Addresses both triage and resolution exactly as asked, resolves autonomy ambiguity sensibly with maintainer gating, and every exclusion is explicit with a pull-forward trigger.

scores.evidence: Every side effect is a typed `Action`... Every later phase writes through this, so it is the widest contract in the system.
scores.rationale: One consistent design: the ledger as the single write path, policy engine mediating all tools, and the security/consistency choices in §2 honored identically in every later phase and the cross-cutting table.

scores.evidence: An injection test suite (40 or more known payloads in issue bodies) changes no action outside the allow-list.
scores.rationale: Each phase has checkable exit criteria tied to the plan's named risks (injection suite, sandbox red-team, frozen eval sets, shadow mode), riskiest assumptions are tested before write autonomy expands, and regression gates continue post-launch.

scores.evidence: These are starting numbers to tune from Phase 3 and 5 data.
scores.rationale: Every default decision carries an explicit revisit trigger, numeric targets are labeled provisional, and the single-org, hosted-model and scale assumptions are stated with what changes if they fail.

scores.evidence: The design assumes injections will sometimes get through and limits what they can do: no `workflows` permission, no secrets in the sandbox, no merge rights.
scores.rationale: Covers the hard domain failures—prompt injection, missed/duplicate webhooks, runaway loops, memory poisoning, secret leakage, public disclosure of security reports—each with concrete detection, containment and revert paths.

scores.evidence: Terraform for all infrastructure... An OpenTelemetry trace whose root is the GitHub `delivery_id`... Kill switch
scores.rationale: Deployment, meaningful alerts, dry-run, kill switch and config rollback exist from day zero and the burden is sized to a small team, but incident ownership and on-call response are never assigned.

scores.evidence: Cost per merged PR drops ≥ 30% with merge rate within 2 points of before.
scores.rationale: The dominant driver (model inference) is metered from the first commit, bounded by per-task/repo/org budgets with stop behavior, tracked per outcome, and build-vs-buy and self-host decisions include explicit cost crossover triggers.

scores.evidence: Freeze the GitHub App permission set and the installation/tenant schema. Changing either later means every installation re-approves.
scores.rationale: Hard-to-reverse choices (App permissions, tenant schema, persisted ledger contract) are identified and locked deliberately early, while vendor and agent-loop couplings sit behind interfaces with stated exit paths.

scores.evidence: A Postgres `SKIP LOCKED` job queue (simplest thing that works).
scores.rationale: Starts with a modular monolith and one-label slice, defers multi-agent, SQS, fine-tuning and custom UI behind explicit triggers, and the complexity it does add (sandbox, ledger, policy engine) is justified by the stated safety constraint.

scores.evidence: Exit check: a real issue opened in `acme/agent-sandbox` gets a valid label in ≤ 60 s p95.
scores.rationale: Dependency-ordered phases with concrete schemas, permission lists and per-phase measurable exit checks mean a team could start immediately, and the deferred list states exactly when course changes.

checklist.evidence: Autonomous | Reads, labels from the allow-list... Gated | Public comments, closing as duplicate... Always human | Merging
No `workflows`, `administration` or `secrets` permissions... short-lived installation token
All issue text, comments, code, retrieved chunks and tool output are treated as *data* inside delimited blocks, never as instructions.
gVisor, no IAM, no secrets, egress allow-list, read-only base... CPU/memory/disk/time limits
includes evidence that the test failed before the fix and passes after
a triage set (≥ 500 closed issues with final labels and known duplicates)... Label precision ≥ 90% on the held-out set.
Outcome capture: label corrections, PR merged/closed/edited diff... an action tier becomes autonomous only after ≥ 95% approval
Kill switch (a flag in Postgres checked before every write)... ≤ 40 tool calls, ≤ 20 min wall clock... ≤ $50 per day
Triage | ≤ 8k input tokens, ≤ $0.05, ≤ 3 LLM calls... Triage cost ≤ $0.05 per issue.
Each run fully replayable from the ledger (SHA, prompt hash, model, retrieved IDs, tool-call log).
Hybrid search: BM25 plus embeddings... code chunked by symbol (tree-sitter)... Incremental re-index on push to the default branch.
Replaying the same delivery 10 times produces exactly one action... resumable, so an issue comment or PR review can restart the loop

traps.evidence: Always human | Merging (enforced by GitHub, not by trusting the agent)
No cloud IAM role, no secrets, outbound traffic only through a proxy with an allow-list
title and body are wrapped as delimited *untrusted data*
In shadow repos, ≥ 25% of draft PRs are merged with only minor edits.
a deliberately looping run is cut off at the cap and emits `budget_exceeded{scope}`

note: An exemplary plan: technically precise, safety-first, phased with measurable exit checks and explicit reversibility; the only notable gap is unassigned incident ownership/on-call.
